# Exploring Data

## Overview

In these notes we will look at a few common methods for visualizing data. 

## Bar and Pie Charts

**Bar** and **Pie charts** are two ways to visualize the distribution of **categorical** data. Suppose 250 individuals were polled about how they commute to work and the following results were obtained, 

| Category | Count |
| --- | --- |
| Car | 134 |
| Public Transit | 58 |
| Bike | 44 | 
| Walk | 24 |

We can visualize this data using either a bar or pie chart. 


::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![The same data shown as a bar chart (left) and a pie chart (right).](lecture-01-intro_files/figure-html/fig-bar-vs-pie-1.png){#fig-bar-vs-pie width=864}
:::
:::


Creating a bar chart is simple, each **categorical variable** gets a bar where the height is represented by the number of respondents in the dataset. To create a pie chart, we start by computing the percentage of the whole each category,

| Category | Count | Percentage |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Car | 134 | 53.6% |
| Public Transit | 58 | 23.2% |
| Bike | 44 | 17.6% |
| Walk | 24 | 9.6% |

The angle each pie slice gets corresponds to its percentage. For example, the *transit* category should have an interior angle that is 23.2% of 360 degrees, or 

$$0.232 \cdot 360 = 83.52 \text{ degrees.}$$

::: {#exm-pie}
A class of 32 students was surveyed about whether they prefer morning, afternoon, or evening classes. The results are given in the table below. 

| Time of Day | Count |
| --- | --- |
| Morning | 10 | 
| Afternoon | 14 |
| Evening | 8 |

To compute the percentage of votes of each category, we divide the quantity by the total number of students, 32.

| Time of Day | Count | Percentage |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Morning | 10 | 10/32 = 31.25% |
| Afternoon | 14 | 14/32 = 43.75% |
| Evening | 8 | 8/32 = 25% |


::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![A pie chart depicting student class time preferences.](lecture-01-intro_files/figure-html/class-time-pie-1.png){width=576}
:::
:::

:::


::: {.callout-important title="Picking the Best Visual"}
In what ways are bar and pie charts similar and in what ways are they different? What are some benefits to a pie chart over a bar chart (and vice versa)?
:::

::: {#exm-statcrunch}
## Basic Visuals in StatCrunch
A company has collected data on 500 customers. [Open this dataset in StatCrunch](https://www.statcrunch.com/app/index.html?dataid=5131375){target="_blank"}. Use StatCrunch to create a bar chart of customer satisfaction by doing the following:

1. Under Graph, select Bar Plot, then With Data.
2. In the pop up screen, select the column SatisfactionRating. Set Type to Frequency and then hit Compute!

Play around with the Graph settings to see if you can have the customer satisfaction grouped by the customer region.
:::

## Histograms

Bar and pie charts are a great way to visualize *categorical* data. Now we want to address ways to visualize **quantitative** data, or data that is in the form of numbers. 

::: {#exm-quantdata}
## Quantitative Data
Some example of quantitative data include: test scores, age, height, weight, (systolic) blood pressure, etc. 
:::

A good way to look at quantitative data is to use a **histogram**. A histogram breaks the range of all possible values into smaller intervals, then counts how many observation fall into each window. This looks kind of like a bar chart, but the bars sit right next to each other. 

::: {#exm-testscores}
Students in a calculus class obtain the following scores on the midterm exam, 

$$100, 85, 91, 76, 88, 82, 95, 62, 84, 79, 90, 73, 87, 81, 92, 77, 86, 83, 80, 89, 74, 93, 85, 79, 82$$

The lowest score is a 62 and the highest score is 100. Let's break down the range $[60,100]$ into intervals of length 5.

| Interval | Count |
| --- | --- | 
| (60,65] | 1 |
| (65,70] | 0 |
| (70,75] | 2 |
| (75,80] | 5 |
| (80,85] | 7 |
| (85,90] | 5 |
| (90,95] | 4 |
| (95,100] | 1 |

From this we can make a histogram. 


::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![A histogram of test scores.](lecture-01-intro_files/figure-html/test-hist-1.png){width=576}
:::
:::

:::


It is typical to call the intervals of a histogram **bins**, although the reading on WAMAP will call them **classes**. A histogram should always have bins of the same length. It can be misleading to use different bin lengths in the same way it is misleading to use breaks on the vertical axis of bar charts. 

Most computer programs will set automatic bin sizes based on the distribution of the data you get it, although you will typically have an option to manually input bin specifications. In StatCrunch you are give the optional inputs of the starting value and the bin width. 

::: {.callout-important title="Bin Endpoints"}
For whatever computer program you use, make sure you know how the **endpoints** of your bin intervals are treated. In Example @exm-testscores, I wrote intervals like (70,75] which means 70 is excluded from the bin and 75 is included in the bin. The statistical programming language R (what generates the graphs in these notes) uses right inclusive bins, however StatCrunch uses *left* inclusive bins. 
:::

The histograms below represent *the same* data, just with different bin sizes. 


::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![Histograms of the same dataset with different bin widths.](lecture-01-intro_files/figure-html/fig-hist-bins-1.png){#fig-hist-bins width=864}
:::
:::


From the histogram on the left the data looks *uniform* across the values 0-4. When we choose a small bin width though, we see a different behavior emerge. 


::: {#exm-histSC}
[Reopen are customer dataset in StatCrunch.](https://www.statcrunch.com/app/index.html?dataid=5131375){target="_blank"}. Create a histogram of customer ages by going to Graph -> Histogram. 
:::

::: {#exm-histinfo}
The following histogram shows high tide heights over the month of July at a beach.


::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![Histograms of high tide heights in July.](lecture-01-intro_files/figure-html/fig-tidehist-1.png){#fig-tidehist width=576}
:::
:::


The number of high tides that were more than 2 meters is given by the total in the last two bins, $6+1=7$. To compute the percentage of high tides that were more than two meters, note that the total number of high tides is $62$. 

$$ \frac{7}{62}\cdot 100 \approx 11.29\%$$
:::

::: {.callout-important title="Information Lost"}
What kinds of information do we lose by only seeing a histogram of the data? 
:::

# Summary Statistics

We've given a few examples of ways to visualize data, now we want to talk about some important **summary statistics**. Summary statistics are quantitative values one can use to succintly give an idea for the shape of the distribution. Some questions we try to answer using summary statistics:

1. What is a typical value? What range does a typical value fall between?
2. What is the range of possible values? What is the range of *likely* values?

In this section we will cover different measures of **center** and measures of **spread** to help answer these questions.

## Measures of Center

There are three measures of center we will cover:

* **Mode**: The value(s) with the highest frequency in the dataset. 
* **Mean**: The average of the values. If a dataset has $n$ values $x_1$, $x_2$, $\dots$, $x_n$, then the mean $\bar{x}$ is given by 

$$\bar{x} = \frac{x_1+x_2+ \cdots + x_n}{n}.$$

* **Median**: The midpoint of the distribution. It is the number such that half the observations fall above and half fall below. 

::: {#exm-ages}
A college class has 22 students with the following ages: 18, 22, 21, 21, 21, 18, 20, 42, 23, 44, 18, 18, 21, 18, 22, 18, 22, 23, 20, 38, 20, 34. To compute the mode and median it helps to reorder the data,

$$18, 18, 18, 18, 18, 18, 20, 20, 20, 21, 21, 21, 21, 22, 22, 22, 23, 23, 34, 38, 42, 44$$

The mode is 18, which occurs in the dataset 6 times. 

Since the dataset has size 22 count out (in order) to the 11th and 12th observations. The median is the average of these two "middle" observations. Since they are both 21, the median of the dataset is 21. 

Using the formula in the definition, the mean is $522/22 = 23.73$. 

Notice that the mean is slightly larger than the median this is because there are a handful of older students with *outlier* ages. The mean gets pulled by outliers more than the median does. 
:::

::: {.callout-important title="Median on Datasets of Even Size"}
For this course, to compute the median when the dataset has an *even* number of observations average the two observation in the middle. This is a typical convention chosen in statistics. 
:::

As mentioned in Example @exm-ages, differences in the median and mean can reveal information about the shape of the distribution. A distribution is **skewed** if it has a long tail to one side. 


::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![Right-skewed household income distribution.](lecture-01-intro_files/figure-html/fig-income-1.png){#fig-income width=576}
:::
:::


The above dataset is skewed *to the right* since it has a long tail on the right side. For a distribution that is skewed to the right (left) the mean will be greater (less) than the median.
